title: The Pet Plan Needs a Backup Human
subtitle: Daily Read | Two friends can make an emergency plan more reliable by rehearsing who can reach the pet, where to find its supplies, and what to do if the owner is away.
imageAlt: Two friends calmly practice placing a cat carrier beside the apartment exit while a cat watches from a nearby shelf.
imageConcept: Two friends in a lived-in apartment, one checking a carrier and a small pet go-bag near the exit while the other writes contact details on a card; a relaxed cat observes from a safe perch.
body: A checklist can’t open the door

Pet emergency plans often begin with supplies: food, medication, a leash, a carrier. Those matter, but they don’t answer a more immediate question: if the person who knows the pet best is not home, who can reach it and take the next step? A useful plan connects one animal to one capable backup person, with clear access, instructions and a destination. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention recommends arranging a buddy system, keeping a carrier or leash near an exit, and learning where a frightened pet might hide [1]. The Federal Emergency Management Agency also encourages people to plan with friends, neighbors or relatives and to get pets familiar with carriers and car travel before an emergency [2].

This is not a test of devotion or preparedness. It is a calm handoff rehearsal: two friends make the plan together, then check whether the person stepping in could actually use it. The goal is not to predict every emergency. It is to reduce the number of decisions someone has to make while worried and short on time.
Choose the backup before you need one

Start by asking the pet’s owner whom they trust to enter the home and help. A nearby friend, neighbor or relative may be a practical choice, but the backup needs to be willing, reachable and able to do the agreed tasks. Confirm whether they have a key, building access or another approved way in. If access depends on a code or lockbox, agree where that information will be kept and how it can be shared securely.

Be specific about the handoff. Does the backup agree to collect the pet only if the owner is away? Can they transport the animal? Are they able to care for it for a few hours or overnight? Who is the alternate if the first person is unavailable? Write names and phone numbers on a paper copy as well as saving them on a phone. FEMA advises planning with people who can help and identifying a pet-friendly destination ahead of time [2]. A plan that assumes someone will be free, without asking them, is not yet a plan.
Learn the pet’s version of the floor plan

Walk through the home together at an ordinary pace. Ask the owner where the pet tends to retreat when startled: under a bed, behind furniture, in a closet, or somewhere less obvious. The backup should know what the pet looks like and what name it responds to, but avoid assuming that a frightened animal will come when called. CDC guidance specifically recommends learning where pets may hide when they are scared [1].

Notice the practical route from that likely hiding place to the exit. Is the carrier easy to reach? Is it blocked by stored items? Can a door be closed to limit the pet’s movement while the carrier is prepared? If there are multiple pets, note whether they travel together or need separate carriers. The point is not to stage a dramatic chase; it is to spot avoidable obstacles while there is time to move a carrier or clear a path. Respect the animal’s temperament, and don’t force a practice that makes it more distressed.
Make the carrier familiar, not frightening

A carrier that appears only during stressful trips can be harder to use in a hurry. If the pet is comfortable with it, leave it accessible in a familiar area and let the animal investigate at its own pace. The owner can reward calm approaches or, when appropriate, practice a short carrier-and-transport routine. CDC recommends carrier practice, and FEMA also advises helping pets become familiar with carriers and car travel before an emergency [1][2].

The backup person should learn the owner’s usual approach: where the carrier opens, how it latches, and whether a towel or other familiar item is useful. Don’t turn this into a timed drill or insist that a nervous animal be picked up. If the pet shows signs of distress, pause and let the owner decide whether to try another day or ask a veterinarian for guidance. The useful rehearsal is the human handoff—knowing what to do and where things are—not making the animal perform.
Pack for the handoff, not just the shelf

Together, identify a small go-bag or a clearly marked spot for essentials. Depending on the pet’s needs, that might include food, water, leash or harness, medication, waste bags, familiar comfort items, and copies of relevant records. FEMA recommends keeping evacuation supplies ready and reviewing food and medicine [2]. CDC also advises preparing a pet go-kit and keeping identification and records current [1].

Check that the backup can find the supplies without asking the owner to remember every location. Make a one-page note with the pet’s name, routine or handling details that matter during transport, medication instructions as provided by the owner or veterinarian, the owner’s contact information, and a veterinary contact. Add a recent photo that could help identify the pet if separated. Keep sensitive information accessible only to the people who need it. Revisit the contents when food, medication or contact details change, rather than assuming a packed bag stays useful indefinitely.
Choose the destination and the first call

A backup needs somewhere to take the pet. The owner and friend can identify a preferred destination—such as a trusted person’s home, pet-friendly lodging or another suitable location—and a second option in case the first is unavailable. Check the current rules and practical details before relying on a destination: whether pets are accepted, how to reach it, and whether the animal’s carrier or records will be needed.

Write down the first calls to make and the order in which to make them. That may include the owner, an alternate contact and the destination. Keep the plan simple enough to use under pressure; a short list is easier to scan than a long explanation. CDC recommends choosing a pet-friendly destination and arranging a buddy system [1]. The Texas Department of Insurance likewise advises identifying caregivers or pet-friendly destinations and keeping a pet kit accessible [3]. The two friends should agree what the backup can decide independently and what requires the owner’s approval when communication is possible.

A pet plan must never ask someone to trade human safety for an animal rescue. If a fire makes it unsafe to retrieve a pet, leave and stay out; tell emergency responders where the animal may be inside. The Texas Department of Insurance states this guidance directly [3]. Put it in the written plan, and say it aloud during the rehearsal so there is no ambiguity about the priority.

That rule also clarifies why knowing a pet’s likely hiding place matters: the backup can give responders useful information without re-entering. If the owner is away, the friend’s job is to follow emergency instructions, get to safety and communicate what they know. For other emergencies, follow local authorities’ directions about whether to evacuate or shelter in place. A written pet plan supports emergency guidance; it does not replace it.
Rehearse the handoff on a quiet day

Set aside ten or fifteen unhurried minutes. Have the owner show the backup the carrier, supplies, access method and likely hiding place. Ask the backup to point out the destination and contacts without being prompted. Then talk through one scenario: “You’re not home, I get the alert, and I can reach the pet—what happens first?” If a step is unclear, change the note or the setup rather than relying on memory.

Before you finish, make sure both people know where the plan lives and how to reach the other person if a phone is unavailable. Agree on a simple review trigger, such as a move, a new medication, a changed phone number or a change in who can provide care. This is not a timed test, and it does not need to be repeated until it feels perfect. A short, accurate handoff is more useful than an elaborate plan no one can find.
Leave the plan ready for the person who isn’t there

At your next calm moment together, let the backup person take the lead through the written plan: show where they would enter, find the carrier, locate the go-bag and identify the destination. The owner can fill in gaps, but try not to narrate every step in advance. Note what the friend could find on their own and what still depends on the owner explaining it. Make one practical change—move a blocked carrier, update a number or clarify a contact—and then save the revised plan where both people can access it. The measure of a good rehearsal is not how smooth it looks with everyone present; it is whether the next person knows what to do when the owner is not.
